analysis.one_liner: Raises the government's burden of proof before it can permanently take someone's property through civil asset forfeiture.
analysis.headline: The civil forfeiture reform bill drew 94 bipartisan cosponsors but never received a vote in any House committee or on the floor before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current federal law, the government can seize cash, cars, and homes through civil forfeiture without convicting, or even charging, the owner of a crime. This bill would make the government prove its case with 'clear and convincing evidence' instead of the much lower 'preponderance' standard, require proof that the owner actually knew of or facilitated the misuse of their property, guarantee a lawyer to people fighting a seizure, and send forfeiture proceeds to the Treasury's general fund instead of back to law enforcement budgets. It also raises the bar for seizing cash on suspicion of 'structuring' — depositing money in small amounts to dodge reporting rules — a practice that has swept up small businesses and people who did nothing illegal.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary property owners — especially people whose cash, vehicles, or homes are seized on suspicion without a criminal charge. It would also help cash-intensive small businesses, such as restaurants and convenience stores, whose bank deposits have been seized under structuring laws. Anyone contesting a forfeiture would get a court-appointed lawyer regardless of whether the property is their home.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Owners of seized property and small businesses

how_it_helps.text: Raises the government's burden of proof in federal civil forfeiture from a preponderance of the evidence to clear and convincing evidence, making it materially harder to keep seized property [S2][S3].

Requires the government to prove the owner used the property to facilitate an offense, or knowingly consented or was willfully blind to such use — protecting innocent owners whose property is taken because of someone else's alleged crime [S2][S3].
Guarantees a person contesting a civil forfeiture legal representation without regard to whether the property is being used as their primary residence [S2][S3].
Redirects forfeiture proceeds from Justice Department accounts to the Treasury's General Fund, removing the financial incentive for agencies to seize property [S2][S3].

Adds a 'knowingly' requirement to the structuring offense and gives anyone whose cash is seized on a structuring suspicion a probable-cause hearing within 14 days, with the money returned if the government cannot show probable cause [S2][S3].
Expands the factors courts weigh in deciding whether a forfeiture is unconstitutionally excessive, including the hardship to the property owner and their dependents [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement agencies, which currently keep most forfeiture proceeds to fund operations, training, and equipment through the Department of Justice Assets Forfeiture Fund and shared arrangements with state and local police. Prosecutors would also face a higher evidentiary bar and additional hearings in forfeiture cases.

drawbacks.text: Prosecutors argue forfeiture is a key tool for dismantling drug trafficking and financial crime, and the bill would make it harder to strip criminal enterprises of their assets — the government must now prove more, not just that property was connected to an offense [S2][S3].

Sending forfeiture proceeds to the Treasury's General Fund rather than Justice Department accounts would cut off a funding stream that currently pays for law enforcement activities, and agencies would lose a revenue source tied to their caseloads [S2][S3].
The added hearing and proof requirements would increase the time and cost of forfeiture proceedings for federal agencies and courts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is honest: making it harder to take property means fewer wrongful seizures of innocent people's cash and homes, but also more work for prosecutors to reach the assets of actual criminals. The bill tilts toward the property owner — and its design tackles the root conflict of interest by cutting the money that flows back to the seizing agency. The cost falls on enforcement budgets and the pace of asset-stripping, not on innocent people.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees and then to subcommittees, sat there without a markup or a floor vote, and expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Walberg (R-MI) introduced the FAIR Act on January 27, 2015, joined by original cosponsors from both parties including Reps. Cárdenas (D-CA), Ellison (D-MN), Garrett (R-NJ), and McClintock (R-CA) [S1][S3].
The bill was referred to the Judiciary Committee plus three others — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Financial Services — splitting it among committees with no path forward designated [S5].
In its first weeks it was sent to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations and the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, where it stayed [S5].
It attracted 94 cosponsors — 40 Democrats and 54 Republicans [S4] — but no committee ever voted on it and it never reached the House floor before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies and prosecutors are better off: the rules that let them keep and spend forfeiture proceeds, and the low burden of proof behind them, stayed in place.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was genuinely bipartisan — 40 Democrats and 54 Republicans cosigned — and the bill's failure was not a party vote but committee inaction: no chamber ever voted on it.

industries.industry: Federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies
industries.note: Federal civil forfeiture currently recycles seized cash and property back into law enforcement budgets through the DOJ Assets Forfeiture Fund and shared payments to local police. The bill would send those proceeds to the Treasury instead and raise the proof needed to keep seized property — directly cutting the revenue and legal leverage agencies rely on. Their interest in keeping the system runs against property owners' interest in keeping their property.

The bill raises the evidentiary standard, adds owner-knowledge requirements, mandates prompt hearings for structuring seizures, and expands proportionality review, all of which make forfeiture cases harder and slower to win.

industries.industry: Property owners and cash-intensive small businesses
industries.note: Restaurants, convenience stores, and other cash businesses are frequent targets of structuring-based seizures; the bill requires proof of intent and a probable-cause hearing within 14 days, with money returned if the government falls short.
